newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Chileans are winners in lackluster Colombia power.
newsitem.headline: Chileans are winners in lackluster Colombia power.

text.p: Chilean companies have emerged as the big winners in the first phase of Colombia's power plant privatization program.
But the Colombian government, particularly its Mines and Energy Ministry, fared less well -- it only managed to find buyers for three of the generators on the auction block.

The Energy Trade and Finance Corporation, a subsidiary of Chile's Chilgener, bought the 1,000 megawatt (MW) Chivor hydro- electric plant, in central Colombia, Friday after submitting a winning bid of 644.5 billion pesos. Chivor is one of Colombia's biggest generators and now the largest in private hands.

The day before, the Endesa-Colombia consortium, composed of Chile's Endesa and 25 percent Colombian finance company Corfivalle, snapped up a 99 percent of the 499 MW Betania hydro- electric generator, in the southwest, for 302 billion pesos.

"We're proud to announce that two Chilean companies have teamed up with Colombia to provide electricity generating services," Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said at an event to reveal the results of the Chivor bidding process.
The Mines and Energy Ministry scrapped the sell-off of the 150 megawatt coal-fired Termotasajero plant Thursday, saying no suitable bid had been submitted.

And it was forced to scrap the sale of three others Friday -- the gas and oil-fired Yumbo, Gualanday and Ocoa plants, all with a 40 megawatt capacity -- after no bids were submitted. All three are curently run by the state-owned oil company Ecopetrol.
The government's 14.25 percent stake in the gas and oil-fired Termocartagena generator, on the Caribbean coast, was sold Thursday to Venezuela's Electricidad de Caracas for 2.6 billion pesos.
Eighty percent of Colombia's power comes from hydro-electric generators.

Many of the country's remaining thermo-electric generators were built as a safety mechanism in the event of the hydro-electric stations failing. Nine foreign companies, from Chile, Venezuela, Germany, Spain and Britain, had submitted valid bids for the privatization process.

Endesa general manager Jaime Bauza told Reuters he was working on a plan to restructure Betania's debt which stand at about $200 million. Investment bank JP Morgan is helping to restructure tha plant's financial plan, which Bauza said would probably consist of extended debt repayment periods and negotiating more favorable interest rates.
"The (Betania) power plant is in good shape. It's been well- managed and the rules of the game in Colombia's energy sector are very stable which is why we entered the market," Bauza said.
He explained the 302 billion peso purchase price for Betania had been covered with Endesa's own funds and with some foreign credit, which he did not specify.
Chilgener executives declined to comment after the purchase of Chivor.
